group.passage: The pandemic has brought about changes, both in good and bad ways. For example, online shopping has skyrocketed, but [[1]] the number of returns—about a quarter of orders! The return rate is further worsened by a “bracketing” strategy. By “bracketing strategy,” shoppers [[2]] of free shipping and returns, which occurs on the premise of bulk buying. Therefore, bargain hunters tend to buy various sizes or colors of a certain product, return the rest, and only keep the ones they like. But have you ever wondered where all those returned products go? Will they be sanitized and reshelved? [[3]] some companies do resell products on other retail channels, most companies choose to avoid handling the returns altogether by either gifting them to customers or simply throwing them away. For companies, they may as well let consumers keep the undesired products, but it is not so ideal because this will create more waste in the landfills. How about simply dumping them? After all, to reshelve a product, companies have to first [[4]], and then sterilize them before they can be resold, which is a very laborious and costly process. A business executive revealed that his company made profits of nearly $400 million from online sales in 2021, but spent $385 million in processing returns. [[5]]? Buy only what you definitely need and you are doing a big favor in reducing the waste.
